'''''Musa balbisiana''''', also known simply as '''plantain''', is a [[wild-type]] species of [[banana]]. It is one of the ancestors of modern cultivated bananas, along with ''[[Musa acuminata]]''.

==Description==
It grows lush leaves in clumps with a more upright habit than most cultivated bananas.  Flowers grow in [[inflorescence]]s coloured red to maroon.  The fruit are between blue and green. They are considered inedible because of the seeds they contain.

==Taxonomy==
It was first scientifically described in 1820 by the Italian botanist [[Luigi Aloysius Colla]].<ref name=powo/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Borborah |first1=Kongkona |last2=Borthakur |first2=S. K. |last3=Tanti |first3=Bhaben |date=2016-06-23 |title=A new variety of Musa balbisiana Colla from Assam, India |url=https://www.banglajol.info/index.php/BJPT/article/view/28348/18870 |journal=Bangladesh Journal of Plant Taxonomy |language=en |volume=23 |issue=1 |pages=75–78 |doi=10.3329/bjpt.v23i1.28348 |issn=2224-7297|doi-access=free }}</ref>

==Distribution==
It is native to eastern [[South Asia]], the eastern regions of the [[Indian subcontinent]], northern [[Southeast Asia]], and southern [[China]]. Introduced populations exist in the wild, far outside its native range.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Perrier|first1=Xavier|last2=Langhe|first2=Edmond De|last3=Donohue|first3=Mark|last4=Lentfer|first4=Carol|last5=Vrydaghs|first5=Luc|last6=Bakry|first6=Frédéric|last7=Carreel|first7=Françoise|last8=Hippolyte|first8=Isabelle|last9=Horry|first9=Jean-Pierre|last10=Jenny|first10=Christophe|last11=Lebot|first11=Vincent|date=2011-07-12|title=Multidisciplinary perspectives on banana (''Musa'' spp.) domestication|journal=[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]]|language=en|volume=108|issue=28|pages=11311–11318|doi=10.1073/pnas.1102001108|pmc=3136277|pmid=21730145|bibcode=2011PNAS..10811311P|doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Uses==
It is assumed that wild bananas were cooked and eaten, as farmers would not have developed the cultivated banana otherwise. Seeded ''Musa balbisiana'' fruit are called ''butuhan'' ('with seeds') in the [[Philippines]],<ref>{{cite web|url= http://www.bananacrop.com/2010/01/progenitors-of-edible-bananas-in.html|title= Progenitors of Edible Bananas|date= November 1, 2010|publisher= Guide to Growing Bananas |access-date= January 12, 2011|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20110707210203/http://www.bananacrop.com/2010/01/progenitors-of-edible-bananas-in.html|archive-date= July 7, 2011}}</ref> and ''kluai tani'' (กล้วยตานี) in [[Thailand]],<ref>{{cite book|title =Plant use in Southern Thailand|publisher=Chiang Mai University|url =http://archive.lib.cmu.ac.th/full/T/2005/biol0805uu_ch4.pdf|archive-url =https://web.archive.org/web/20140413143722/http://archive.lib.cmu.ac.th/full/T/2005/biol0805uu_ch4.pdf|archive-date =2014-04-13}}</ref> where its leaves are used for packaging and crafts.<ref name="BP-20190819">{{cite news |last1=Karnjanatawe |first1=Karnjana |title=Going bananas |url=https://www.bangkokpost.com/life/social-and-lifestyle/1732779/going-bananas |access-date=19 August 2019 |work=Bangkok Post |date=19 August 2019}}</ref> Natural [[Parthenocarpy|parthenocarpic]] clones occur through [[polyploidy]] and produce edible bananas, examples of which are wild [[saba banana]]s.<ref name="a3">{{cite web |url= http://www.plantnames.unimelb.edu.au/Sorting/Musa.html|title= Sorting Musa names|author= Michel H. Porcher| author2 = Prof. Snow Barlow| date= July 19, 2002|publisher= The University of Melbourne |access-date= January 11, 2011}}</ref>

==Genome==
''Musa balbisiana'' contributed the B [[genome]] to the cultivated banana.<ref name="Genome"/>

Wang ''et al.'', 2019 provides a [[genome]], [[evolution]]ary analysis and [[functional genomics]] analysis.<ref name="Genome"/> Wang ''et al.'' find evolution increasing [[ethylene]] production in the domesticated form.<ref name="Genome">
